target_customer: Banks that wanted to offer developer APIs to their corporate clients
problem: Banks lacked modern APIs, so corporate customers could not integrate treasury and accounting systems directly. Standard Treasury built white-labeled API platforms for banks.
business_model: B2B software sold to banks, hosted and maintained API platform

founders.name: Daniel Kimerling
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (2013) says he previously built Giftly.

founders.name: Zac Townsend
prior_employers: Office of Newark Mayor Cory Booker (technology policy, then CTO of Newark per YC page)
founders.background_notes: YC page: later inaugural Chief Data Officer of California and CEO of Meanwhile.

founders.name: Brent Goldman
founders.background_notes: Listed as a founder on the YC page; the 2015 SVB acquisition coverage names only Kimerling and Townsend.

exit.reason: Acqui-hire and asset purchase; the founders said regulatory and geographic risks left them unable to raise a Series A.

competitors.name: FIS Global
competitors.what: Publicly traded vendor of banking and payments technology sold to banks

technical_complexity.rationale: Required integrating with bank core systems for checks, transfers, account opening and FX with strong security, which is hard for a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Deep bank integration creates lock-in, but sales cycles were long and the idea was replicable by banks or larger vendors.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: SVB bought the team and assets in August 2015 to build its own API platform.

market_need_then: Developer platforms from firms like Stripe and Braintree showed demand for API driven finance, while banks offered little programmatic access. At launch it was piloting with one of the five largest US banks.

brand_strength.rationale: Sources show little brand activity; the name signals credibility to banks but is generic.

outcome_analysis: Standard Treasury sold API middleware to banks and raised a 2.7M seed. It concluded the full vision required its own bank, and regulatory and geographic risks left it unable to raise a Series A, so it was acqui-hired with assets by Silicon Valley Bank in August 2015. The result was a soft landing for the team rather than a venture return; the exit price was not disclosed.
notes: Seed amount from the YC blog (announced May 2014, closed late 2013); investor list from a search summary of aggregator data, partly unverified. Directory has no website; none was found. Brent Goldman is on the YC page but aggregators differ on cofounders. Education not found for any founder.
